title: How do you create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)?
shortTitle: How to create an immutable class in Java (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies)
keyPoints: Make the class final so no subclass can add mutable behaviour.
Make all fields private and final, assigned exactly once in the constructor.
Provide no setters or any mutating methods; return a new object for changes.
Defensively copy mutable fields both on the way in (constructor) and out (getters).
Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe, safe to cache, and make reliable map keys.
BigDecimal and String are already immutable; Java records simplify immutable class creation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Make the class final, all fields private final and set once, no setters, and defensively copy anything mutable coming in or going out.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Immutable class** – an instance whose state cannot change after construction.
- **Five rules** – final class, private final fields, no setters, initialise in constructor, defensive copies of mutable fields.
- **Thread safety** – since nothing can change, many threads can read concurrently without locks.
- **Safe caching** – share one instance freely without fear of aliasing bugs.
- **Map keys** – hash code and equality never change, so immutable objects are reliable map keys and set elements.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a completed transaction receipt at National Bank of India. Once the receipt is printed showing Rajesh transferred fifty thousand rupees to Priya on a given date, nobody can go back and alter the amount or the date on that receipt. If you need a different amount, you print a brand-new receipt; you never edit the old one. An immutable class works the same way: once created, its contents are frozen forever.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Five Rules for Immutability
  ───────────────────────────

  Rule 1: final class
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ public final class TransferRecord │ ◄── no subclass can add mutable state
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Rule 2: private final fields
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ private final String txnId;      │
  │ private final BigDecimal amount; │ ◄── assigned once, never reassigned
  │ private final List<String> tags; │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Rule 3: no setters
  Rule 4: initialise in constructor
  Rule 5: defensive copy

  Constructor (in):            Getter (out):
  tags = List.copyOf(tags)     return Collections.unmodifiableList(tags)
       ▲                             ▲
       │                             │
  Caller cannot mutate       Caller cannot mutate
  via original reference     via returned reference
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An immutable class is one whose objects cannot change state after construction. Rajesh creates one by following five rules. He makes the class final so no subclass can add mutable behaviour. He makes all fields private and final so each is assigned exactly once. He provides no setters. He initialises every field in the constructor. And the subtle one: he defensively copies any mutable fields both on the way in and on the way out.

The defensive-copy rule is the part that trips people up. If a field is a mutable object like a `List`, storing the caller's reference directly is dangerous because the caller still holds that reference. In the constructor Rajesh copies it with `List.copyOf`, and in the getter he returns an unmodifiable view. Fields like `String` and `BigDecimal` are already immutable and need no copy.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj made the `TransferRecord` immutable because a completed transfer is shared across the notification, reporting, and reconciliation systems. If any of those could accidentally change the amount, the bank's books would become inconsistent. By freezing the record, Pankaj hands the same object to many systems concurrently with no locks. When a modified version is needed, a "with" method returns a brand-new record.

The benefits are thread safety without locks, safe sharing and caching, and reliable use as map keys. The one trade-off is that producing new objects for every change can create garbage under heavy load. But for correctness and safety, particularly with money, immutability is the strong default, and it is exactly how Java's own `String`, `BigDecimal`, and records are designed.

Remember one sentence: make the class final, all fields private final, no setters, and defensively copy anything mutable in and out.
